On Teachers' Day at Ishita's school, Uma ma'am brought a big tin of laddoos she had made herself. "My first try," she said shyly, handing them round the classroom.
Ishita bit into one. It was hard as a stone and tasted of too much ghee. Around her, a few children pulled faces.
Uma ma'am was looking right at her. "How is it, Ishita?"
Ishita swallowed. Mummy always said to tell the truth. But ma'am's eyes looked so hopeful.
"I love it, ma'am!" she said.
Uma ma'am beamed and put another one on her desk.
On the way home Ishita felt warm and a little wobbly inside. She had made ma'am happy. But she hadn't told the truth, and now there was a second laddoo in her bag.

qa.q: What did Uma ma'am bring on Teachers' Day?
qa.a: A big tin of laddoos she had made herself.

qa.q: Why did Ishita say 'I love it, ma'am'?
qa.a: Ishita felt torn; she cared about Uma ma'am's hopeful eyes and didn't want to hurt her, so kindness won over the truth for a moment.

qa.q: What true and kind thing could Ishita have said instead?
qa.a: Something like 'Thank you for making them for us, ma'am', which is warm without pretending.

qa.q: How might Uma ma'am feel if she learned the laddoos were too hard?
qa.a: Uma ma'am might feel a little embarrassed, but could also be glad to know, so her next batch turns out better.

grounding: Shows a child praising a teacher's laddoos to avoid hurting her, and feeling the pull between truth and kindness.

passage:
After school in Nabha, Trisha pulled a folded paper from her bag at the chai stall. "I wrote a poem for the district contest. Read it. Honestly."
Parveen read it. The rhymes were forced, and the last verse made no sense. "It's really good," she said. "I loved the ending."
Trisha's face lit up. "Really? I was so nervous."
"Really," Parveen said, and sipped her chai too fast.
It was the third time this month. She had said she was fine when Trisha asked why she'd been so quiet. She had said Trisha's new haircut was nice. Each time it was easier than the awkward conversation.
Walking home, Parveen realised she didn't actually know whether Trisha would still like her if she said what she really thought. And Trisha didn't really know her either. The contest was next week.

qa.q: What did Trisha ask Parveen to read?
qa.a: A poem she wrote for the district contest.

qa.q: Why did Parveen say she loved the ending?
qa.a: Parveen felt awkward and wanted to dodge an uncomfortable moment, so praise felt easier than honest feedback.

qa.q: What could Parveen still do before the contest?
qa.a: Tell Trisha kindly which lines work and suggest looking again at the last verse, so Trisha gets real help in time.

qa.q: What does Trisha lose from Parveen's easy praise?
qa.a: Trisha loses useful feedback before the contest and, slowly, a friend who tells her what she truly thinks.

grounding: Shows a teenager telling a friend her poem is good to avoid awkwardness, and noticing the habit is replacing real closeness.

passage:
After the inter-school dance competition in Kochi, Elizabeth came off stage breathless. She had missed two counts and nearly slipped in the turn.
Her friend Kashish hugged her. "You were amazing! Best in the whole show!"
Her mother said the same. So did her aunt on the phone. Elizabeth let herself believe it. That night she replayed the compliments, warm and happy.
The next day the results went up on the school noticeboard. Elizabeth was eleventh out of twelve.
She stood there, cheeks burning. Had everyone been lying? Or had they just not been watching?
At lunch she asked Kashish, "Did I really look good?"
Kashish hesitated. "I mean... you tried really hard."
Elizabeth nodded slowly. "Next time, can you tell me what went wrong? Otherwise I don't know what to fix."

qa.q: Where did Elizabeth place in the results?
qa.a: Eleventh out of twelve.

qa.q: How did Elizabeth feel when she saw the results?
qa.a: Elizabeth felt embarrassed and confused, cheeks burning, wondering whether everyone had been lying.

qa.q: What did Elizabeth ask Kashish for, and why does it help?
qa.a: Honest feedback next time about what went wrong, so praise becomes information she can actually use.

qa.q: Why might Kashish have said 'You were amazing'?
qa.a: Kashish likely wanted to comfort her friend in the moment, not realising it would leave Elizabeth confused later.

grounding: Shows a teenager warmed by praise for a weak performance, then confused by the results, learning that uncalibrated praise is not usable.

passage:
Student counsellor's note, Thursday
Jomon (second year) came in saying he feels "weirdly lonely" in a flat of five friends.
As we talked, a pattern appeared. He tells his flatmate Manjula he loves her cooking when he doesn't. He says "no problem" when people borrow his laptop, and it is a problem. He laughs at jokes he finds mean. He said, "I just want everyone to be comfortable."
Then he said something important: "But now I don't know if any of them actually like me, or just the version that agrees with everything."
I told him a kind fib now and then does no harm, but when it becomes the only way he speaks, nobody gets to know the real Jomon. We picked one small true thing to try this week: telling Manjula, kindly, that he'd rather she asked before borrowing his charger.
He looked nervous, but agreed. We'll meet again next Thursday.

qa.q: What does Jomon tell Manjula about her cooking?
qa.a: He tells her he loves her cooking when he doesn't.

qa.q: How is Jomon feeling in the flat, and why?
qa.a: Jomon feels weirdly lonely, unsure whether anyone likes the real him or only the version that agrees with everything.

qa.q: What small step did the counsellor and Jomon choose?
qa.a: Telling Manjula kindly that he'd rather she asked before borrowing his charger, one small true thing to try that week.

qa.q: How might Manjula react if Jomon starts saying what he really thinks?
qa.a: Manjula might be surprised at first, but could come to know and trust the real Jomon better.

grounding: Shows a young adult whose many small polite untruths have left him unsure who really likes him, as noted by a counsellor.

passage:
"So?" Irfan held up his phone. "My first wedding shoot as a photographer. Be honest. Actually, don't. Just say it's good."
Uma scrolled through the photos slowly. Some were blurry. The couple's faces were in shadow in half of them.
"Uma?"
"I can see how much work went into this," she said. "And you got the grandmother laughing, look. That's a moment people will keep forever."
Irfan grinned. "And the rest?"
"Do you want the rest?"
He paused. "Yes. Okay. Yes."
"The light was behind them in the garden ones. Next time, maybe turn them round to face it."
He groaned, then laughed. "I knew it. Thanks. Seriously."
"The grandmother one, though," Uma said. "Print that one big."

qa.q: Which moment did Uma point out in the photos?
qa.a: The grandmother laughing.

qa.q: What was Irfan feeling as he handed over the phone?
qa.a: Irfan felt nervous and exposed, half asking for honesty and half hoping just to hear it was good.

qa.q: How did Uma keep both care and honesty?
qa.a: She began with something true and warm, the effort and the grandmother's laugh, then gave the harder feedback only when Irfan asked for it.

qa.q: What would change if Uma had just said 'It's all perfect'?
qa.a: Irfan would feel good briefly but repeat the backlighting mistake at the next shoot.

grounding: Shows an adult replacing a false compliment with something true and warm about effort and a real strength, keeping care and honesty together.

passage:
Daycare note, Tuesday
At snack time a glass fell and broke near the water table. Damini (5) was standing right beside it, eyes very wide. Before anyone asked, she pointed at Tenzin and said, "He did it! Not me!"
Tenzin had been across the room at the blocks.
Damini's hands were tight fists, and she kept looking at the door as if she was waiting for shouting.
What I did: I knelt down and said softly, "Glasses break. Nobody is going to shout. Are you okay?" She burst into tears and whispered, "I did it." I thanked her for telling me, and we swept up together. I told Tenzin sorry for the mix-up.

qa.q: Where did the glass break?
qa.a: Near the water table.

qa.q: Why did Damini point at Tenzin?
qa.a: Damini was frightened and expected shouting, so blaming Tenzin was a panicked way to escape.

qa.q: What helped Damini tell the truth?
qa.a: The teacher knelt, spoke softly, said nobody would shout, asked if she was okay, and thanked her for telling.

qa.q: How might Tenzin have felt being blamed?
qa.a: Tenzin, who was across the room at the blocks, might have felt confused and upset until the teacher said sorry.

grounding: Shows a young child blaming another child for a broken glass out of fear of shouting, a panicked escape rather than a plan.

subtype: Covering a mistake or bad marks [Actor]
passage:
Madhav's maths test said 9 out of 25 in red ink, and it had to come back signed by tomorrow. Mummy was on night shift at the hospital and wouldn't be home till morning.
He sat at the table under the flickering tube light, heart thumping. He practised her signature on scrap paper eleven times. The twelfth looked almost right. He signed.
The next day Ms Rao looked at it a second too long. "Your mother usually signs in blue," she said. "This is black."
"She... used my pen," Madhav said. Then he had to ask his sister Binita to say Mummy had borrowed his pen, in case Ms Rao called.
By evening he had three lies to remember and a stomach ache. Binita looked at him across the dinner table. "Just tell Mummy," she whispered. "It's getting too big."

qa.q: What did Madhav's maths test say?
qa.a: 9 out of 25 in red ink.

qa.q: How did Madhav feel by evening?
qa.a: Madhav felt anxious and weighed down, with three lies to remember and a stomach ache.

qa.q: What would help Madhav most now?
qa.a: Telling Mummy the truth when she is home, as Binita suggested, before more lies are needed to hold up the first one.

qa.q: How might Binita feel being asked to help cover the lie?
qa.a: Binita seems worried and uncomfortable, which is why she whispers that it's getting too big.

grounding: Shows a child forging a signature on a low mark out of shame, and each cover-up needing another lie that grows the fear.

passage:
"Abhinav, Sharma aunty's window has a crack. Do you know anything about it?"
"No, Papa. It was already like that."
Baljeet sat down on the step so his face was level with his son's. "You look scared."
Abhinav stared at his slippers.
"Are you scared I'll shout?"
A small nod.
"I'm not going to shout. I promise. Whatever happened, I'd much rather know the truth."
There was a long silence. Then: "My ball hit it. I didn't mean to."
"Thank you for telling me. That was brave." Baljeet squeezed his shoulder. "Now let's go and tell Sharma aunty together, and I'll help you save from your pocket money for the glass."
"You're not angry?"
"A window can be fixed. I want you to always be able to tell me things."

qa.q: What did Abhinav first say about the window?
qa.a: 'It was already like that.'

qa.q: What was Abhinav feeling while staring at his slippers?
qa.a: Abhinav was scared that Papa would shout, which is why the first answer was a lie.

qa.q: What did Baljeet do that made the truth cheaper than the lie?
qa.a: He got down to Abhinav's level, named the fear, promised not to shout, thanked him for the truth, and made a calm plan to repair the window together.

qa.q: What would change if Baljeet had shouted at the first lie?
qa.a: Abhinav would likely have stuck to the lie and learnt to hide things better, instead of telling the truth.

grounding: Shows a father meeting his son's fearful lie calmly, naming the fear and thanking him for the truth, which makes honesty cheaper than a cover-up.

passage:
I'm Harish, and for most of Class 11 I lied to my parents about Zeenat.
She's my best friend. We do physics together at the library and talk about everything. But in Class 9, when I told my parents about a girl I'd been paired with for a project, Papa laughed at dinner and called her "your girlfriend" in front of my uncles for months. Mummy started checking my phone.
So when Zeenat and I became friends, I just didn't say. I said I was at "group study". I deleted her messages every night.
I'm not proud of it. But I don't think I lied because I'm a liar. I lied because telling the truth last time cost me so much.
Last month I tried again, carefully, with Mummy alone. She listened this time. She asked if Zeenat's parents knew. I said yes. That was a start.

qa.q: What did Harish say instead of mentioning Zeenat?
qa.a: That it was 'group study'.

qa.q: Why did Harish feel the need to hide the friendship?
qa.a: Harish felt ashamed and wary after being mocked at dinner in Class 9, so the truth no longer felt safe.

qa.q: What step helped Harish start being honest again?
qa.a: Trying again carefully with Mummy alone, where it was quieter and she was willing to listen.

qa.q: How might Mummy see the lie now that she knows the background?
qa.a: Mummy might see that the lie came from past ridicule and phone checks, and that making the truth safe matters more than punishment.

grounding: Shows a teenager hiding a friendship because past honesty brought ridicule and control, so the lie reflects how unsafe the truth felt.

passage:
In the college hostel common room, Kishore's phone lit up: "Amma calling." He stepped into the corridor.
"Beta, did the company confirm your joining date? Appa has told the whole family."
"Next week, Amma. They're finalising." There was no company. He had failed three papers and hadn't sat for placements at all.
He hung up and leaned against the wall. The story had started small in January, one "I did fine" after an exam. Now there was a job, a salary, a city. Every call needed more details.
Rehana, the final-year student who ran the peer support desk, stopped beside him. "You okay? You look like you're going to be sick."
Kishore laughed weakly. Then, to his own surprise, he told her everything.
"That's a heavy thing to carry alone," Rehana said. "The counsellor is in till five. Want me to walk you there?"
He nodded.

qa.q: How many papers had Kishore failed?
qa.a: Three papers.

qa.q: What was Kishore feeling as he leaned against the wall?
qa.a: Kishore felt trapped and sick with dread, as the small January lie had grown into a job, a salary and a city.

qa.q: What did Rehana do that helped?
qa.a: She noticed he looked unwell, listened, named it as heavy to carry alone, and offered to walk him to the counsellor right away.

qa.q: How might Amma and Appa feel if the truth comes out later rather than now?
qa.a: They would likely feel shocked and hurt, especially after Appa told the whole family, and the longer it goes on the harder it gets.

grounding: Shows a student in a high-expectation family claiming a job while failing, and the gap between story and reality becoming a trap.
